title: SYSK Gets Weird Playlist: What was the Philadelphia Experiment?
summary: A special guest-produced edition of Stuff You Should Know, part of the "SYSK Gets Weird" playlist, examining the Philadelphia Experiment, a conspiracy theory claiming the US Navy made the destroyer USS Eldridge invisible and teleported it in 1943. The hosts trace the story to Carl M. Allen (Carlos Miguel Allende) and his letters to UFO author Morris K. Jessup, the annotated book that Office of Naval Research researchers received, Jessup's 1959 suicide, and the 1979 book Project Invisibility. They cover the rebuttals: degaussing (demagnetizing ships against magnetic mines), the Eldridge being in Brooklyn per the ship's log, the Navy's fast canal transit, the Engstrom electrician Edward Dudgeon's explanations, the 1999 Eldridge reunion, and the ONR explanation of the green glow as coronal discharge from a later Timmerman test. The episode closes with listener mail from a University of Georgia student, Bailey Johnson, asking for podcasting advice.

segments.title: Opening banter and guest producer
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a special edition with guest producer Noel, and the hosts banter about the 1984 Philadelphia Experiment movie, its 80s special effects, and cast.

segments.title: Movie banter and Eddie and the Cruisers
segments.summary: The hosts joke about 1980s films, Nancy Allen, Michael Pare's role in Eddie and the Cruisers, and the real John Cafferty and the Beaver Brown Band.

segments.title: The experiment as described in the legend
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck describe the claimed July 1943 invisibility experiment on the USS Eldridge in Philadelphia, the October repeat where the ship supposedly reappeared in Norfolk and ten minutes earlier in Philadelphia, the crew's injuries, and the supposed link to Einstein's unified field theory, which the hosts say is not true.

segments.title: Carl Allen's letters to Morris Jessup
segments.summary: Carlos Miguel Allende (Carl M. Allen) wrote about 50 letters to UFO author Morris Jessup claiming to have witnessed the experiment. Jessup asked for evidence, Allen had none, and Allen's claims were largely conjecture and confabulation.

segments.title: ONR visit and annotated UFO book
segments.summary: Two Office of Naval Research researchers visited Jessup in 1957 after receiving his annotated book, annotated by Allen in several hands. They later published an annotated edition of about 127 copies through a contractor, Vero Technologies, and forged copies are reportedly in circulation.

segments.title: Jessup's death and the Eldridge's later fate
segments.summary: Jessup died by suicide in a car exhaust in the late 1950s after injury, divorce, and money trouble; friends said he was deeply depressed. The hosts note conspiracy theorists' claims about it. The Eldridge was transferred to Greece as the HS Leon and scrapped in the 1990s.

segments.title: The Eldridge was in Brooklyn and Dudgeon's rebuttal
segments.summary: The ship was in Brooklyn, not Philadelphia, on the day in question, per the ship's log. Astrophysicist Jacques Vallée tried to disprove the hoax, and in 1994 an ex-Navy electrician named Edward Dudgeon, who served on the USS Engstrom, responded and explained the supposed disappearances in a bar as underage sailors leaving through a back door.

segments.title: Degaussing and rapid transit explanations
segments.summary: Hosts explain degaussing, which wrapped ships in cable to neutralize their magnetism against magnetic mines and torpedoes, and how the Navy's military-only canal could make the round trip quickly, so the ship's apparent disappearance could have been a normal trip. They discuss how rumors grew like a game of telephone.

segments.title: Robert Gorman and Alfred Bialik
segments.summary: Robert Gorman tracked down Carl Allen's family in a 1980 Fate magazine article and found his merchant seaman papers. After the movie, Alfred Bialik claimed to have been a physicist on the Eldridge and to have time-traveled to 1983, and he also claimed ties to the Montauk Project.

segments.title: Green glow explanation and the 1999 reunion
segments.summary: The green glow is often explained as St. Elmo's fire or as coronal discharge from a later Navy test on the USS Timmerman. The Eldridge crew held a 1999 reunion in Atlantic City, where they joked about the story, and the ship's log confirmed it was in Brooklyn.

segments.title: Why the legend endures
segments.summary: Hosts discuss reasons the legend has lasted: Vallée's theory that movies and photos give people something to point to, the 1979 book Project Invisibility, the Navy's declassified human experiments, and the Einstein and suicide angles. They also note how the legend's believers have fared.

segments.title: Hosts' skepticism and closing verdict
segments.summary: Hosts discuss enjoying conspiracy theories without believing them, then give two reasons the story can't be true: no teleportation has been developed since, and Robert Gorman's quote calling the story an implausible naval act. They recommend the HowStuffWorks search for more.

segments.title: Listener mail from Bailey Johnson
segments.summary: Bailey Johnson, a University of Georgia student who started listening in seventh grade, asks for advice on starting a campus podcast. The hosts advise good microphones, a reliable release schedule, conversational scripting or a shared outline, and interesting topics.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
